slides.title: Silent chest. Paradoxical breathing. SpO2 falling.

slides.pearl: Complete laryngospasm can be totally silent.

slides.body: Tight mask seal. Remove the stimulus and gently suction secretions.
Firm pressure at the laryngospasm notch (Larson's maneuver) while holding positive pressure.
Small IV dose of propofol if the spasm persists.
If severe or not breaking. Be ready to intubate. Watch for bradycardia, especially in children.

slides.title: Don't wait for stridor.
slides.body: Treat early, before hypoxemia turns an airway problem into a cardiac one.

caption:
Silent chest, paradoxical breathing, SpO2 falling. Would you call it laryngospasm in under 10 seconds? 🫁

Swipe for the 4-step response: 100% O2 and help → jaw thrust + CPAP at the laryngospasm notch → deepen with propofol → small-dose succinylcholine if it won't break.

💡 Complete laryngospasm can be silent. Don't wait for stridor.

question: First drug?
why: Restores SVR and diastolic pressure without pushing heart rate up. The thick LV needs that pressure to perfuse its own coronaries.
pearl: In severe AS, hypotension AND tachycardia are both the enemy.
caption:
Severe AS. BP 70/40, HR 92, two minutes after induction. What are you pushing first? 🫀

Answer in the Reel, but comment your pick before you watch it 👇

The hypertrophied LV is perfusion-dependent: keep SVR and diastolic pressure up, keep the rate normal, protect sinus rhythm.

scene: Just intubated. Breath sounds on the RIGHT only.
question: Most likely cause?
why: Check depth at the teeth, deflate the cuff, withdraw slowly while listening, and confirm bilateral breath sounds.
pearl: Check tube depth first. Fastest fix, most common cause.
caption:
SpO2 86% right after intubation, breath sounds on the right only. What's your first check? 🫁

The right mainstem bronchus is shorter, wider, and more vertical. Always check the tube depth before chasing anything else.

scene: Laparoscopic chole. HR drops as the abdomen inflates.
question: What's happening?
why: Peritoneal stretch triggers a vagal reflex. Ask the surgeon to release pressure, then give an anticholinergic if bradycardia persists.
pearl: Bradycardia with insufflation: release the pressure first, then treat.
caption:
HR drops to 48 the moment the abdomen inflates. What's your move? 🎃

Peritoneal stretch can trigger a strong vagal response. Talk to the surgeon: release the pneumoperitoneum, then treat with glycopyrrolate or atropine if it persists. Always consider CO2 embolism if ETCO2 or BP crash suddenly.

scene: ETCO2 drops from 38 to 12 in two breaths.
question: Most likely?
why: With BP falling too, think embolism, massive bleeding, or arrest. Take two seconds to check the circuit, then treat the patient.
pearl: Gradual fall = ventilation. Abrupt fall + hypotension = perfusion. Flat zero = disconnection.
caption:
ETCO2 crashes from 38 to 12 in two breaths, BP 74/40. Equipment or patient? 📉

An abrupt drop with hypotension points to falling cardiac output: PE, air embolism, hemorrhage, or arrest. Rule out the circuit in seconds, then treat the patient.
